Based on the search results, the **second most powerful earthquake ever recorded** was the **1964 Great Alaska earthquake** (also called the Prince William Sound earthquake or Good Friday earthquake) with a magnitude of **9.2**.

Regarding deaths, different sources report slightly different numbers due to varying accounting methods and data availability at the time:

- **USGS**: Reports **130 people died**
- **Quartz**: States **"about 131"** total deaths
- **Live Science**: Notes **"128 lives"** lost

The generally accepted figure is approximately **130 people killed**, though some estimates range from 128–131. This death toll is remarkably low given the earthquake's massive size, largely because the affected coastline was relatively thinly populated at the time. Most fatalities were caused by tsunamis rather than the shaking itself.

For comparison, the largest earthquake ever recorded was the 1960 Valdivia earthquake in Chile (magnitude 9.5), which killed approximately 1,655 people.

A handful of regions around the world regularly unleash terrifyingly large earthquakes. Here are the 21 largest earthquakes on record.

As the world's tectonic plates crash, grind and dive into one another, they release their pent-up energy in giant earthquakes that can rock the ground, trigger volcanic eruptions, move mountains and unleash tsunamis.
And since scientists figured out how to measure earthquake magnitude in the early 1900s, some truly massive quakes have shaken our planet. These are the monstrous "megathrust" earthquakes, the most powerful quakes in the world. A huge fraction of these earthquakes occurred in a handful of subduction zones along the seismically restless "Ring of Fire" in the Pacific, where tectonic plates dive beneath one another.
From the devastating Sumatran quake and tsunami of 2004 to a monstrous temblor in Siberia that, thankfully, killed no one, here are the 20 largest earthquakes ever recorded, according to the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS).

# The 21 largest recorded earthquakes in history
## 21. Sanriku-Oki, Japan; 1933; magnitude 8.4
1933 Sanriku Earthquake damage at Kamaishi, Japan.
(Image credit: By Unknown author - Japanese magazine "Historical Photograph, April 1933 issue" published by Rekishi-Shasin Kai., Public Domain)
A magnitude 8.4 quake struck near the Sanriku region of Japan on March 2, 1933, according to the USGS. The quake occurred about 180 miles (290 kilometers) offshore of Honshu, Japan.
Most of the deaths resulted from the tsunami the quake generated, which swept away 3,000 homes and destroyed 2,000 others and generated nearly 100-foot (29 meters) waves in Honshu, Japan.

Several decades later, a magnitude 9.0 temblor would rock the same general region, causing the Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami of 2011.
This area is part of the Pacific Ring of Fire, a nearly 25,000-mile-long (40,000 km) horseshoe-shaped belt that is known for both earthquakes and volcanic activity. The ring fringes the boundaries of the Pacific Plate wherever it smashes into its neighboring plates; in the region around Tōhoku, the Pacific Plate is colliding with the North American Plate.

# The 21 largest recorded earthquakes in history
## 20. Arequipa, Peru; 2001; magnitude 8.4
Map showing the location of the Arequipa earthquake in Peru (2001).
(Image credit: USGS)
A magnitude 8.4 earthquake struck 4 miles (6 km) from the coastal town of Atico, Peru, on June 23, 2001. At least 74 people were killed; more than a third of them were swept away by the resulting tsunami. More than 2,600 people were injured, and over 50,000 homes were damaged by the strong ground shaking.
The quake occurred at the boundary of the Nazca and South American plates, where the Nazca Plate is moving northeast at about 3 inches (78 millimeters) per year, smashing into and diving beneath the South American Plate, according to the USGS. Ground shaking as a result of the seismic activity was felt as far away as La Paz, Bolivia.

# The 21 largest recorded earthquakes in history
## 19. South of Sumatra, 2007, magnitude 8.4
A family sits near their quake damaged home in Lais village, about 50 km from Bengkulu City, on September 13, 2007, in Bengkulu province, Sumatra Island, Indonesia.
(Image credit: Dimas Ardian / Stringer via Getty Images)
On April 12, 2007, a magnitude 8.4 earthquake struck approximately 76 miles (122 km) offshore of Bengkulu, Indonesia, on the island of Sumatra. The giant quake occurred due to thrust faulting on the boundary between the Sunda and Australian plates.

Around 25 people died, and more than 161 were injured. More than 20,000 buildings were damaged in the cities of Bengkulu and Sumatera Barat, according to the USGS.
The quake marked the fourth magnitude 7.9 or greater temblor to strike the general region that decade; the area was still actively remodeling itself after the monster quake that struck just after Christmas Day in 2004 (see #3).

# The 21 largest recorded earthquakes in history
## 18. Near Kamchatka Peninsula, 1923, magnitude 8.4
Here we see the location of the 1923 earthquake near the Kamchatka Peninsula, Russia.
(Image credit: USGS)
Relatively little is known about the magnitude 8.4 quake that struck off the east coast of Kamchatka, Russia, on Feb. 3, 1923. The sparsely populated area of the Russian Far East sits near the Kuril-Kamchatka Trench, where the Pacific Plate is diving beneath the Okhotsk Plate, a teensy plate that was once thought to be part of the North American Plate.
No reported injuries or deaths occurred, but the quake triggered a modest tsunami, according to the USGS.

# The 21 largest recorded earthquakes in history
## 5. Kamchatka Peninsula, Russia; 1952; magnitude 9.0
Kamchatka Krai Russia, is home to one of the most active volcanic regions in the world.
(Image credit: ISS Crew Earth Observations experiment and Image Science & Analysis Laboratory, Johnson Space Center)
The world's first recorded magnitude 9.0 earthquake struck off the east coast of Kamchatka on Nov. 4, 1952. The quake generated a 43-foot (13 m) tsunami locally. The tsunami rocked Crescent City, California.
No one died, but in Hawaii, property damage was estimated at up to $1 million ($11.12 million in today's dollars). The waves tossed boats onto the beach, caused houses to collide, destroyed piers, scoured beaches and moved road pavement.

# The 21 largest recorded earthquakes in history
## 4. Tōhoku, Japan; 2011; magnitude 9.1
Earthquake damage shown after the devastating magnitude 9.0 Tōhoku earthquake taken in Kesennuma, Miyagi prefecture 11 days after the major temblor struck the island nation.
(Image credit: Paula Bronstein/Getty)
On March 11, 2011, a magnitude 9.1 quake triggered a tsunami that left more than 15,700 people dead, more than 4,600 missing, over 5,300 injured and more than 130,900 displaced, according to the USGS. More than 332,000 buildings, 2,100 roads, 56 bridges and 26 railways were damaged as a result of the quake. The quake also damaged nuclear reactors at the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant, leading to one of the biggest nuclear disasters in history. This earthquake was the largest ever recorded in Japan, and cost an estimated $309 billion in damage.
For weeks afterward, strong aftershocks above magnitude 6.0, and even 7.0, continued to rock the region, and the quake sent tsunami waves as far as Hawaii, California and the Galapagos Islands. Even in distant Antarctica, the quakes cracked large slabs of ice from the Sulzberger Ice Shelf, according to the USGS.
The quake was caused by thrust faulting near the Japan Trench, the boundary between the Pacific and North American plates.

# The 21 largest recorded earthquakes in history
## 3. Sumatra-Andaman Islands, 2004, magnitude 9.1
An aerial view of the devastated coastline to the south of Banda Aceh city, Indonesia, some 8 months after the 2004 Indian Ocean Earthquake and Tsunami. The powerful waves striped bare the flat coastal plains causing immense loss of life and total devastation of coastal properties and farmlands.
(Image credit: Photography by Mangiwau via Getty Images)
This quake was the third-largest earthquake in history and the largest since the 1964 earthquake in Prince William Sound, Alaska (see #2). In total, nearly 300,000 people were killed or presumed dead, and about 1.2 million people were displaced by the earthquake and subsequent tsunami in 10 countries in Southeast Asia and East Africa.
Extremely strong shaking was felt in Banda Aceh, but the deadliest aspect of this quake was the resulting tsunami, which caused more deaths than any other in recorded history up to that point. The tsunami was recorded nearly worldwide on tide gauges in the Indian, Pacific and Atlantic oceans.
The massive quake struck one day after Christmas along the interface of the Indian and Burma tectonic plates and was caused by the release of stress that developed as the Indian Plate dived beneath the Burma microplate. The massive fault zone, which was offshore, was as long as California, according to the USGS.

# The 21 largest recorded earthquakes in history
## 2. Prince William Sound, Alaska; 1964; magnitude 9.2
Devastation from the 1965 Prince William Sound earthquake.
(Image credit: USGS)
This great earthquake and ensuing tsunami took 128 lives and caused about $311 million in property loss. The earthquake damage was heavy in many towns, including Anchorage, which was about 75 miles (120 km) northwest of the epicenter. The quake, which struck on March 27, 1964, ruptured along a seismically active fault between the North American and Pacific plates. The shaking lasted about 3 minutes.
Landslides in Anchorage caused heavy damage. Huge slides occurred in the downtown business section, and water mains and gas, sewer, telephone and electrical systems were disrupted throughout the area.

# The 21 largest recorded earthquakes in history
## 1. Valdivia, Chile; 1960; magnitude 9.5
Wrecked houses in Valdivia, Chile after the 1960 earthquake.
(Image credit: USGS)
Approximately 1,655 people died in the largest earthquake ever recorded, which struck Valdivia, Chile, on May 22, 1960. Thousands more were injured, and millions were left homeless. Southern Chile suffered $550 million in damage.
The quake triggered a tsunami that killed 61 people in Hawaii, 138 in Japan and 32 in the Philippines.
The earthquake struck where the Nazca Plate dives underneath the South American Plate, on the Peru-Chile Trench.

Updated October 20, 2026
Illustration: Quartz
A magnitude 9.0 earthquake releases roughly 32 times more energy than a magnitude 8.0, and about 1,000 times more than a 7.0. That logarithmic math is why the small group of ruptures above magnitude 8.5 sits in a category of its own. The thousands of other damaging earthquakes logged since seismic networks began keeping score do not come close. The gap between an 8.5 and a 9.5 is not a matter of degree. It is a difference in the physical size of the fault that broke, the length of time the ground moved and the volume of seawater displaced.
The strongest earthquakes in recorded history were not always the deadliest. Death tolls depend on population density, construction standards, the time of day and whether the rupture pushed up a tsunami. A magnitude 8.7 in an uninhabited stretch of the North Pacific can pass with no confirmed fatalities. A far weaker quake beneath a crowded city can kill tens of thousands. Raw energy release and human loss are two separate measurements, and they rarely line up.
This list covers the instrumental era, generally from 1900 onward, because that is when seismic networks became capable of assigning reliable numbers. Earthquakes described in older historical records may have matched or exceeded these, but without seismographs there is no way to measure them. The magnitudes here come from the moment magnitude scale, which replaced the Richter scale for large events. It calculates energy release from the physical dimensions of the fault rupture and the amount of slip, rather than from shaking recorded at a single station.
One pattern runs through nearly every entry. These ruptures occurred along subduction zones, where one tectonic plate grinds beneath another. The boundary locks in place for decades or centuries, then releases the stored strain in a few minutes. Chile, Alaska, Sumatra, Japan and Kamchatka appear repeatedly for that reason. Knowing which boundaries have produced earthquakes this size is the clearest guide to where comparable events remain possible.

## The 1960 Valdivia earthquake in Chile remains the strongest ever recorded
Illustration: Quartz
The magnitude 9.5 earthquake that struck near Valdivia in southern Chile on May 22, 1960, is the most powerful earthquake ever measured by seismic instruments. No recorded event since has matched its energy release.
The rupture tore along the Peru-Chile Trench for a stretch estimated at more than 500 miles, as the Nazca Plate slipped beneath the South American Plate. A fault break of that length is what separates the event from everything below it on the scale. Magnitude depends on rupture area and the amount of slip, and few plate boundaries on Earth hold enough continuous locked fault to produce a break this long.
The rupture pushed a tsunami across the entire Pacific basin. Waves struck the Chilean coast within minutes, then crossed deep water at roughly 500 miles per hour toward Hawaii, Japan and the Philippines. The first destructive waves reached Hilo, Hawaii, about 15 hours later, more than 6,000 miles from the source, and wrecked much of the downtown waterfront. Hilo rebuilt with open parkland along the bayfront instead of commercial blocks.
Casualty figures for the combined earthquake and tsunami vary by source, ranging from about 1,000 to as high as 6,000. The spread reflects how hard it was to count the dead in 1960. Communications were cut across a sparsely settled, heavily damaged stretch of south-central Chile, and some coastal villages were erased outright. Economic losses were severe, with housing, farmland, ports and rail links destroyed across several provinces.
Valdivia remains the benchmark against which every other large earthquake is measured, and it also sets a practical ceiling in seismic hazard modeling. Anything substantially larger would require a locked fault segment longer than any subduction zone known to store strain. That constraint is why 9.5 is often treated as close to the physical limit of crustal rupture.

## The 1964 Alaska earthquake was the second-strongest ever measured
Illustration: Quartz
The magnitude 9.2 earthquake that ruptured beneath Prince William Sound on March 27, 1964, is the second-strongest quake ever recorded and the largest measured in North America. It broke along the Aleutian megathrust, where the Pacific Plate is forced beneath the North American Plate. Many accounts call it the Good Friday earthquake, after the day it struck.
Ground motion continued for four to five minutes across parts of south-central Alaska. That is an extreme duration — most large quakes shake for well under a minute. The sustained motion liquefied unstable ground in Anchorage, roughly 75 miles from the epicenter. Landslides carried away whole blocks of housing in the Turnagain Heights neighborhood and collapsed part of the downtown commercial district.
Tsunamis caused most of the deaths. Waves generated by submarine landslides reached Alaskan fishing communities within minutes of the shaking. The ocean-crossing wave arrived at Crescent City on the northern California coast hours later and killed people there. The combined toll is generally put at about 131 — low for a rupture this size, and a consequence of how thinly populated the affected coastline was in 1964.
The earthquake rearranged the land itself. Surveys afterward found stretches of coast and seafloor lifted by more than 30 feet. Other areas dropped far enough to flood shoreline forests, leaving stands of dead trees in salt water. Geologist George Plafker mapped that pattern of uplift and subsidence. His work showed the rupture had occurred on a shallow-dipping thrust fault. That evidence helped confirm how subduction zones generate the largest earthquakes, at a time when plate tectonics was still being worked out.
The event reshaped warning systems and engineering practice. The U.S. opened a tsunami warning center at Palmer, Alaska, in 1967, after the 1964 waves hit nearby coastlines with no alert. Studies of how Anchorage's slopes and structures behaved during prolonged shaking informed later seismic design standards for soil stability and building performance.

## The 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake triggered one of history's deadliest tsunamis
Illustration: Quartz
A magnitude 9.1 earthquake ruptured the seafloor off the northwest coast of Sumatra on December 26, 2004, breaking more than 900 miles of fault and generating the deadliest tsunami in recorded history.
The fault that failed marks the boundary where the Indian Plate descends beneath the Burma microplate, part of the Sunda subduction system. The seafloor lifted along that entire length. The movement displaced an enormous column of water, which spread outward across the Indian Ocean in every direction.
Waves struck Indonesia's Aceh province within roughly 20 to 30 minutes, destroying whole coastal districts of Banda Aceh. Sri Lanka, southern India and the Thai resort coast were hit within one to two hours. Hours after that, the waves still carried enough force to kill people on the coasts of Somalia and Tanzania, thousands of miles from the epicenter.
The death toll is generally placed at about 230,000 people across 14 countries, with Indonesia accounting for the largest share by far. That figure remains an estimate rather than a count. Many victims were never recovered, and some affected communities had no complete population records to measure the loss against.
Wave height alone does not explain the scale of the disaster. The Indian Ocean had no tsunami warning network comparable to the system already running in the Pacific. Seismologists registered the earthquake quickly, but no mechanism existed to turn that detection into warnings for the coastal populations in the path of the water. Most people standing on the beaches did not know what the sudden retreat of the sea meant.
The Indian Ocean Tsunami Warning System was built in the aftermath, connecting seismic sensors, deep-ocean pressure gauges and national alert channels across the region.
The rupture also shifted enough of Earth's mass to shorten the length of a day by a fraction of a microsecond, according to analyses by geophysicists who modeled the event's seismic data.

That logarithmic math is why the small group of ruptures above magnitude 8.5 sits in a category of its own. The thousands of other damaging earthquakes logged since seismic networks began keeping score do not come close. The gap between an 8.5 and a 9.5 is not a matter of degree. It is a difference in the physical size of the fault that broke, the length of time the ground moved and the volume of seawater displaced.
The strongest earthquakes in recorded history were not always the deadliest. Death tolls depend on population density, construction standards, the time of day and whether the rupture pushed up a tsunami. A magnitude 8.7 in an uninhabited stretch of the North Pacific can pass with no confirmed fatalities. A far weaker quake beneath a crowded city can kill tens of thousands. Raw energy release and human loss are two separate measurements, and they rarely line up.
This list covers the instrumental era, generally from 1900 onward, because that is when seismic networks became capable of assigning reliable numbers. Earthquakes described in older historical records may have matched or exceeded these, but without seismographs there is no way to measure them. The magnitudes here come from the moment magnitude scale, which replaced the Richter scale for large events. It calculates energy release from the physical dimensions of the fault rupture and the amount of slip, rather than from shaking recorded at a single station.
One pattern runs through nearly every entry. These ruptures occurred along subduction zones, where one tectonic plate grinds beneath another. The boundary locks in place for decades or centuries, then releases the stored strain in a few minutes. Chile, Alaska, Sumatra, Japan and Kamchatka appear repeatedly for that reason. Knowing which boundaries have produced earthquakes this size is the clearest guide to where comparable events remain possible.

## The 1960 Valdivia earthquake in Chile remains the strongest ever recorded
Illustration: Quartz
The magnitude 9.5 earthquake that struck near Valdivia in southern Chile on May 22, 1960, is the most powerful earthquake ever measured by seismic instruments. No recorded event since has matched its energy release.
The rupture tore along the Peru-Chile Trench for a stretch estimated at more than 500 miles, as the Nazca Plate slipped beneath the South American Plate. A fault break of that length is what separates the event from everything below it on the scale. Magnitude depends on rupture area and the amount of slip, and few plate boundaries on Earth hold enough continuous locked fault to produce a break this long.
The rupture pushed a tsunami across the entire Pacific basin. Waves struck the Chilean coast within minutes, then crossed deep water at roughly 500 miles per hour toward Hawaii, Japan and the Philippines. The first destructive waves reached Hilo, Hawaii, about 15 hours later, more than 6,000 miles from the source, and wrecked much of the downtown waterfront. Hilo rebuilt with open parkland along the bayfront instead of commercial blocks.
Casualty figures for the combined earthquake and tsunami vary by source, ranging from about 1,000 to as high as 6,000. The spread reflects how hard it was to count the dead in 1960. Communications were cut across a sparsely settled, heavily damaged stretch of south-central Chile, and some coastal villages were erased outright. Economic losses were severe, with housing, farmland, ports and rail links destroyed across several provinces.
Valdivia remains the benchmark against which every other large earthquake is measured, and it also sets a practical ceiling in seismic hazard modeling. Anything substantially larger would require a locked fault segment longer than any subduction zone known to store strain. That constraint is why 9.5 is often treated as close to the physical limit of crustal rupture.
texts.2:
## The 1964 Alaska earthquake was the second-strongest ever measured
Illustration: Quartz
The magnitude 9.2 earthquake that ruptured beneath Prince William Sound on March 27, 1964, is the second-strongest quake ever recorded and the largest measured in North America. It broke along the Aleutian megathrust, where the Pacific Plate is forced beneath the North American Plate. Many accounts call it the Good Friday earthquake, after the day it struck.
Ground motion continued for four to five minutes across parts of south-central Alaska. That is an extreme duration — most large quakes shake for well under a minute. The sustained motion liquefied unstable ground in Anchorage, roughly 75 miles from the epicenter. Landslides carried away whole blocks of housing in the Turnagain Heights neighborhood and collapsed part of the downtown commercial district.
Tsunamis caused most of the deaths. Waves generated by submarine landslides reached Alaskan fishing communities within minutes of the shaking. The ocean-crossing wave arrived at Crescent City on the northern California coast hours later and killed people there. The combined toll is generally put at about 131 — low for a rupture this size, and a consequence of how thinly populated the affected coastline was in 1964.
The earthquake rearranged the land itself. Surveys afterward found stretches of coast and seafloor lifted by more than 30 feet. Other areas dropped far enough to flood shoreline forests, leaving stands of dead trees in salt water. Geologist George Plafker mapped that pattern of uplift and subsidence. His work showed the rupture had occurred on a shallow-dipping thrust fault. That evidence helped confirm how subduction zones generate the largest earthquakes, at a time when plate tectonics was still being worked out.
The event reshaped warning systems and engineering practice. The U.S. opened a tsunami warning center at Palmer, Alaska, in 1967, after the 1964 waves hit nearby coastlines with no alert. Studies of how Anchorage's slopes and structures behaved during prolonged shaking informed later seismic design standards for soil stability and building performance.
texts.3:
## The 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake triggered one of history's deadliest tsunamis
Illustration: Quartz
A magnitude 9.1 earthquake ruptured the seafloor off the northwest coast of Sumatra on December 26, 2004, breaking more than 900 miles of fault and generating the deadliest tsunami in recorded history.
The fault that failed marks the boundary where the Indian Plate descends beneath the Burma microplate, part of the Sunda subduction system. The seafloor lifted along that entire length. The movement displaced an enormous column of water, which spread outward across the Indian Ocean in every direction.
Waves struck Indonesia's Aceh province within roughly 20 to 30 minutes, destroying whole coastal districts of Banda Aceh. Sri Lanka, southern India and the Thai resort coast were hit within one to two hours. Hours after that, the waves still carried enough force to kill people on the coasts of Somalia and Tanzania, thousands of miles from the epicenter.
The death toll is generally placed at about 230,000 people across 14 countries, with Indonesia accounting for the largest share by far. That figure remains an estimate rather than a count. Many victims were never recovered, and some affected communities had no complete population records to measure the loss against.
Wave height alone does not explain the scale of the disaster. The Indian Ocean had no tsunami warning network comparable to the system already running in the Pacific. Seismologists registered the earthquake quickly, but no mechanism existed to turn that detection into warnings for the coastal populations in the path of the water. Most people standing on the beaches did not know what the sudden retreat of the sea meant.
The Indian Ocean Tsunami Warning System was built in the aftermath, connecting seismic sensors, deep-ocean pressure gauges and national alert channels across the region.
The rupture also shifted enough of Earth's mass to shorten the length of a day by a fraction of a microsecond, according to analyses by geophysicists who modeled the event's seismic data.

As the world's tectonic plates crash, grind and dive into one another, they release their pent-up energy in giant earthquakes that can rock the ground, trigger volcanic eruptions, move mountains and unleash tsunamis.
And since scientists figured out how to measure earthquake magnitude in the early 1900s, some truly massive quakes have shaken our planet. These are the monstrous "megathrust" earthquakes, the most powerful quakes in the world. A huge fraction of these earthquakes occurred in a handful of subduction zones along the seismically restless "Ring of Fire" in the Pacific, where tectonic plates dive beneath one another.

A magnitude 8.4 quake struck near the Sanriku region of Japan on March 2, 1933, according to the USGS. The quake occurred about 180 miles (290 kilometers) offshore of Honshu, Japan.
Most of the deaths resulted from the tsunami the quake generated, which swept away 3,000 homes and destroyed 2,000 others and generated nearly 100-foot (29 meters) waves in Honshu, Japan.

# The 21 largest recorded earthquakes in history
## 20. Arequipa, Peru; 2001; magnitude 8.4
Map showing the location of the Arequipa earthquake in Peru (2001).
(Image credit: USGS)
A magnitude 8.4 earthquake struck 4 miles (6 km) from the coastal town of Atico, Peru, on June 23, 2001. At least 74 people were killed; more than a third of them were swept away by the resulting tsunami. More than 2,600 people were injured, and over 50,000 homes were damaged by the strong ground shaking.
The quake occurred at the boundary of the Nazca and South American plates, where the Nazca Plate is moving northeast at about 3 inches (78 millimeters) per year, smashing into and diving beneath the South American Plate, according to the USGS. Ground shaking as a result of the seismic activity was felt as far away as La Paz, Bolivia.

## 19. South of Sumatra, 2007, magnitude 8.4
A family sits near their quake damaged home in Lais village, about 50 km from Bengkulu City, on September 13, 2007, in Bengkulu province, Sumatra Island, Indonesia.
(Image credit: Dimas Ardian / Stringer via Getty Images)
On April 12, 2007, a magnitude 8.4 earthquake struck approximately 76 miles (122 km) offshore of Bengkulu, Indonesia, on the island of Sumatra. The giant quake occurred due to thrust faulting on the boundary between the Sunda and Australian plates.

# The 21 largest recorded earthquakes in history
## 18. Near Kamchatka Peninsula, 1923, magnitude 8.4
Here we see the location of the 1923 earthquake near the Kamchatka Peninsula, Russia.
(Image credit: USGS)
Relatively little is known about the magnitude 8.4 quake that struck off the east coast of Kamchatka, Russia, on Feb. 3, 1923. The sparsely populated area of the Russian Far East sits near the Kuril-Kamchatka Trench, where the Pacific Plate is diving beneath the Okhotsk Plate, a teensy plate that was once thought to be part of the North American Plate.
No reported injuries or deaths occurred, but the quake triggered a modest tsunami, according to the USGS.

# The 21 largest recorded earthquakes in history
## 5. Kamchatka Peninsula, Russia; 1952; magnitude 9.0
Kamchatka Krai Russia, is home to one of the most active volcanic regions in the world.
(Image credit: ISS Crew Earth Observations experiment and Image Science & Analysis Laboratory, Johnson Space Center)
The world's first recorded magnitude 9.0 earthquake struck off the east coast of Kamchatka on Nov. 4, 1952. The quake generated a 43-foot (13 m) tsunami locally. The tsunami rocked Crescent City, California.
No one died, but in Hawaii, property damage was estimated at up to $1 million ($11.12 million in today's dollars). The waves tossed boats onto the beach, caused houses to collide, destroyed piers, scoured beaches and moved road pavement.

# The 21 largest recorded earthquakes in history
## 4. Tōhoku, Japan; 2011; magnitude 9.1
Earthquake damage shown after the devastating magnitude 9.0 Tōhoku earthquake taken in Kesennuma, Miyagi prefecture 11 days after the major temblor struck the island nation.
(Image credit: Paula Bronstein/Getty)
On March 11, 2011, a magnitude 9.1 quake triggered a tsunami that left more than 15,700 people dead, more than 4,600 missing, over 5,300 injured and more than 130,900 displaced, according to the USGS. More than 332,000 buildings, 2,100 roads, 56 bridges and 26 railways were damaged as a result of the quake. The quake also damaged nuclear reactors at the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant, leading to one of the biggest nuclear disasters in history. This earthquake was the largest ever recorded in Japan, and cost an estimated $309 billion in damage.
For weeks afterward, strong aftershocks above magnitude 6.0, and even 7.0, continued to rock the region, and the quake sent tsunami waves as far as Hawaii, California and the Galapagos Islands. Even in distant Antarctica, the quakes cracked large slabs of ice from the Sulzberger Ice Shelf, according to the USGS.
The quake was caused by thrust faulting near the Japan Trench, the boundary between the Pacific and North American plates.

# The 21 largest recorded earthquakes in history
## 3. Sumatra-Andaman Islands, 2004, magnitude 9.1
An aerial view of the devastated coastline to the south of Banda Aceh city, Indonesia, some 8 months after the 2004 Indian Ocean Earthquake and Tsunami. The powerful waves striped bare the flat coastal plains causing immense loss of life and total devastation of coastal properties and farmlands.
(Image credit: Photography by Mangiwau via Getty Images)
This quake was the third-largest earthquake in history and the largest since the 1964 earthquake in Prince William Sound, Alaska (see #2). In total, nearly 300,000 people were killed or presumed dead, and about 1.2 million people were displaced by the earthquake and subsequent tsunami in 10 countries in Southeast Asia and East Africa.
Extremely strong shaking was felt in Banda Aceh, but the deadliest aspect of this quake was the resulting tsunami, which caused more deaths than any other in recorded history up to that point. The tsunami was recorded nearly worldwide on tide gauges in the Indian, Pacific and Atlantic oceans.
The massive quake struck one day after Christmas along the interface of the Indian and Burma tectonic plates and was caused by the release of stress that developed as the Indian Plate dived beneath the Burma microplate. The massive fault zone, which was offshore, was as long as California, according to the USGS.
texts.38:
# The 21 largest recorded earthquakes in history
## 2. Prince William Sound, Alaska; 1964; magnitude 9.2
Devastation from the 1965 Prince William Sound earthquake.
(Image credit: USGS)
This great earthquake and ensuing tsunami took 128 lives and caused about $311 million in property loss. The earthquake damage was heavy in many towns, including Anchorage, which was about 75 miles (120 km) northwest of the epicenter. The quake, which struck on March 27, 1964, ruptured along a seismically active fault between the North American and Pacific plates. The shaking lasted about 3 minutes.
Landslides in Anchorage caused heavy damage. Huge slides occurred in the downtown business section, and water mains and gas, sewer, telephone and electrical systems were disrupted throughout the area.

# The 21 largest recorded earthquakes in history
## 1. Valdivia, Chile; 1960; magnitude 9.5
Wrecked houses in Valdivia, Chile after the 1960 earthquake.
(Image credit: USGS)
Approximately 1,655 people died in the largest earthquake ever recorded, which struck Valdivia, Chile, on May 22, 1960. Thousands more were injured, and millions were left homeless. Southern Chile suffered $550 million in damage.
The quake triggered a tsunami that killed 61 people in Hawaii, 138 in Japan and 32 in the Philippines.
The earthquake struck where the Nazca Plate dives underneath the South American Plate, on the Peru-Chile Trench.

A magnitude 8.7 in an uninhabited stretch of the North Pacific can pass with no confirmed fatalities. A far weaker quake beneath a crowded city can kill tens of thousands. Raw energy release and human loss are two separate measurements, and they rarely line up.
This list covers the instrumental era, generally from 1900 onward, because that is when seismic networks became capable of assigning reliable numbers. Earthquakes described in older historical records may have matched or exceeded these, but without seismographs there is no way to measure them. The magnitudes here come from the moment magnitude scale, which replaced the Richter scale for large events. It calculates energy release from the physical dimensions of the fault rupture and the amount of slip, rather than from shaking recorded at a single station.
One pattern runs through nearly every entry. These ruptures occurred along subduction zones, where one tectonic plate grinds beneath another. The boundary locks in place for decades or centuries, then releases the stored strain in a few minutes. Chile, Alaska, Sumatra, Japan and Kamchatka appear repeatedly for that reason. Knowing which boundaries have produced earthquakes this size is the clearest guide to where comparable events remain possible.

## The 1960 Valdivia earthquake in Chile remains the strongest ever recorded
Illustration: Quartz
The magnitude 9.5 earthquake that struck near Valdivia in southern Chile on May 22, 1960, is the most powerful earthquake ever measured by seismic instruments. No recorded event since has matched its energy release.
The rupture tore along the Peru-Chile Trench for a stretch estimated at more than 500 miles, as the Nazca Plate slipped beneath the South American Plate. A fault break of that length is what separates the event from everything below it on the scale. Magnitude depends on rupture area and the amount of slip, and few plate boundaries on Earth hold enough continuous locked fault to produce a break this long.
The rupture pushed a tsunami across the entire Pacific basin. Waves struck the Chilean coast within minutes, then crossed deep water at roughly 500 miles per hour toward Hawaii, Japan and the Philippines. The first destructive waves reached Hilo, Hawaii, about 15 hours later, more than 6,000 miles from the source, and wrecked much of the downtown waterfront. Hilo rebuilt with open parkland along the bayfront instead of commercial blocks.
Casualty figures for the combined earthquake and tsunami vary by source, ranging from about 1,000 to as high as 6,000. The spread reflects how hard it was to count the dead in 1960. Communications were cut across a sparsely settled, heavily damaged stretch of south-central Chile, and some coastal villages were erased outright. Economic losses were severe, with housing, farmland, ports and rail links destroyed across several provinces.
Valdivia remains the benchmark against which every other large earthquake is measured, and it also sets a practical ceiling in seismic hazard modeling. Anything substantially larger would require a locked fault segment longer than any subduction zone known to store strain. That constraint is why 9.5 is often treated as close to the physical limit of crustal rupture.

## The 1964 Alaska earthquake was the second-strongest ever measured
Illustration: Quartz
The magnitude 9.2 earthquake that ruptured beneath Prince William Sound on March 27, 1964, is the second-strongest quake ever recorded and the largest measured in North America. It broke along the Aleutian megathrust, where the Pacific Plate is forced beneath the North American Plate. Many accounts call it the Good Friday earthquake, after the day it struck.
Ground motion continued for four to five minutes across parts of south-central Alaska. That is an extreme duration — most large quakes shake for well under a minute. The sustained motion liquefied unstable ground in Anchorage, roughly 75 miles from the epicenter. Landslides carried away whole blocks of housing in the Turnagain Heights neighborhood and collapsed part of the downtown commercial district.
Tsunamis caused most of the deaths. Waves generated by submarine landslides reached Alaskan fishing communities within minutes of the shaking. The ocean-crossing wave arrived at Crescent City on the northern California coast hours later and killed people there. The combined toll is generally put at about 131 — low for a rupture this size, and a consequence of how thinly populated the affected coastline was in 1964.
The earthquake rearranged the land itself. Surveys afterward found stretches of coast and seafloor lifted by more than 30 feet. Other areas dropped far enough to flood shoreline forests, leaving stands of dead trees in salt water. Geologist George Plafker mapped that pattern of uplift and subsidence. His work showed the rupture had occurred on a shallow-dipping thrust fault. That evidence helped confirm how subduction zones generate the largest earthquakes, at a time when plate tectonics was still being worked out.
The event reshaped warning systems and engineering practice. The U.S. opened a tsunami warning center at Palmer, Alaska, in 1967, after the 1964 waves hit nearby coastlines with no alert. Studies of how Anchorage's slopes and structures behaved during prolonged shaking informed later seismic design standards for soil stability and building performance.

## The 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake triggered one of history's deadliest tsunamis
Illustration: Quartz
A magnitude 9.1 earthquake ruptured the seafloor off the northwest coast of Sumatra on December 26, 2004, breaking more than 900 miles of fault and generating the deadliest tsunami in recorded history.
The fault that failed marks the boundary where the Indian Plate descends beneath the Burma microplate, part of the Sunda subduction system. The seafloor lifted along that entire length. The movement displaced an enormous column of water, which spread outward across the Indian Ocean in every direction.
Waves struck Indonesia's Aceh province within roughly 20 to 30 minutes, destroying whole coastal districts of Banda Aceh. Sri Lanka, southern India and the Thai resort coast were hit within one to two hours. Hours after that, the waves still carried enough force to kill people on the coasts of Somalia and Tanzania, thousands of miles from the epicenter.
The death toll is generally placed at about 230,000 people across 14 countries, with Indonesia accounting for the largest share by far. That figure remains an estimate rather than a count. Many victims were never recovered, and some affected communities had no complete population records to measure the loss against.
Wave height alone does not explain the scale of the disaster. The Indian Ocean had no tsunami warning network comparable to the system already running in the Pacific. Seismologists registered the earthquake quickly, but no mechanism existed to turn that detection into warnings for the coastal populations in the path of the water. Most people standing on the beaches did not know what the sudden retreat of the sea meant.
The Indian Ocean Tsunami Warning System was built in the aftermath, connecting seismic sensors, deep-ocean pressure gauges and national alert channels across the region.
The rupture also shifted enough of Earth's mass to shorten the length of a day by a fraction of a microsecond, according to analyses by geophysicists who modeled the event's seismic data.

As the world's tectonic plates crash, grind and dive into one another, they release their pent-up energy in giant earthquakes that can rock the ground, trigger volcanic eruptions, move mountains and unleash tsunamis.
And since scientists figured out how to measure earthquake magnitude in the early 1900s, some truly massive quakes have shaken our planet. These are the monstrous "megathrust" earthquakes, the most powerful quakes in the world. A huge fraction of these earthquakes occurred in a handful of subduction zones along the seismically restless "Ring of Fire" in the Pacific, where tectonic plates dive beneath one another.
From the devastating Sumatran quake and tsunami of 2004 to a monstrous temblor in Siberia that, thankfully, killed no one, here are the 20 largest earthquakes ever recorded, according to the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS).

## 20. Arequipa, Peru; 2001; magnitude 8.4
Map showing the location of the Arequipa earthquake in Peru (2001).

A magnitude 8.4 earthquake struck 4 miles (6 km) from the coastal town of Atico, Peru, on June 23, 2001. At least 74 people were killed; more than a third of them were swept away by the resulting tsunami. More than 2,600 people were injured, and over 50,000 homes were damaged by the strong ground shaking.
The quake occurred at the boundary of the Nazca and South American plates, where the Nazca Plate is moving northeast at about 3 inches (78 millimeters) per year, smashing into and diving beneath the South American Plate, according to the USGS. Ground shaking as a result of the seismic activity was felt as far away as La Paz, Bolivia.

## 18. Near Kamchatka Peninsula, 1923, magnitude 8.4
Here we see the location of the 1923 earthquake near the Kamchatka Peninsula, Russia.

Relatively little is known about the magnitude 8.4 quake that struck off the east coast of Kamchatka, Russia, on Feb. 3, 1923. ## 5. Kamchatka Peninsula, Russia; 1952; magnitude 9.0
Kamchatka Krai Russia, is home to one of the most active volcanic regions in the world.
(Image credit: ISS Crew Earth Observations experiment and Image Science & Analysis Laboratory, Johnson Space Center)
The world's first recorded magnitude 9.0 earthquake struck off the east coast of Kamchatka on Nov. 4, 1952. The quake generated a 43-foot (13 m) tsunami locally. The tsunami rocked Crescent City, California.
No one died, but in Hawaii, property damage was estimated at up to $1 million ($11.12 million in today's dollars). The waves tossed boats onto the beach, caused houses to collide, destroyed piers, scoured beaches and moved road pavement.

# The 21 largest recorded earthquakes in history
## 4. Tōhoku, Japan; 2011; magnitude 9.1
Earthquake damage shown after the devastating magnitude 9.0 Tōhoku earthquake taken in Kesennuma, Miyagi prefecture 11 days after the major temblor struck the island nation.
(Image credit: Paula Bronstein/Getty)
On March 11, 2011, a magnitude 9.1 quake triggered a tsunami that left more than 15,700 people dead, more than 4,600 missing, over 5,300 injured and more than 130,900 displaced, according to the USGS. More than 332,000 buildings, 2,100 roads, 56 bridges and 26 railways were damaged as a result of the quake. The quake also damaged nuclear reactors at the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant, leading to one of the biggest nuclear disasters in history. This earthquake was the largest ever recorded in Japan, and cost an estimated $309 billion in damage.
For weeks afterward, strong aftershocks above magnitude 6.0, and even 7.0, continued to rock the region, and the quake sent tsunami waves as far as Hawaii, California and the Galapagos Islands. Even in distant Antarctica, the quakes cracked large slabs of ice from the Sulzberger Ice Shelf, according to the USGS.
The quake was caused by thrust faulting near the Japan Trench, the boundary between the Pacific and North American plates.

# The 21 largest recorded earthquakes in history
## 3. Sumatra-Andaman Islands, 2004, magnitude 9.1
An aerial view of the devastated coastline to the south of Banda Aceh city, Indonesia, some 8 months after the 2004 Indian Ocean Earthquake and Tsunami. The powerful waves striped bare the flat coastal plains causing immense loss of life and total devastation of coastal properties and farmlands.
(Image credit: Photography by Mangiwau via Getty Images)
This quake was the third-largest earthquake in history and the largest since the 1964 earthquake in Prince William Sound, Alaska (see #2). In total, nearly 300,000 people were killed or presumed dead, and about 1.2 million people were displaced by the earthquake and subsequent tsunami in 10 countries in Southeast Asia and East Africa.
Extremely strong shaking was felt in Banda Aceh, but the deadliest aspect of this quake was the resulting tsunami, which caused more deaths than any other in recorded history up to that point. The tsunami was recorded nearly worldwide on tide gauges in the Indian, Pacific and Atlantic oceans.
The massive quake struck one day after Christmas along the interface of the Indian and Burma tectonic plates and was caused by the release of stress that developed as the Indian Plate dived beneath the Burma microplate. The massive fault zone, which was offshore, was as long as California, according to the USGS.

# The 21 largest recorded earthquakes in history
## 2. Prince William Sound, Alaska; 1964; magnitude 9.2
Devastation from the 1965 Prince William Sound earthquake.
(Image credit: USGS)
This great earthquake and ensuing tsunami took 128 lives and caused about $311 million in property loss. The earthquake damage was heavy in many towns, including Anchorage, which was about 75 miles (120 km) northwest of the epicenter. The quake, which struck on March 27, 1964, ruptured along a seismically active fault between the North American and Pacific plates. The shaking lasted about 3 minutes.
Landslides in Anchorage caused heavy damage. Huge slides occurred in the downtown business section, and water mains and gas, sewer, telephone and electrical systems were disrupted throughout the area.

# The 21 largest recorded earthquakes in history
## 1. Valdivia, Chile; 1960; magnitude 9.5
Wrecked houses in Valdivia, Chile after the 1960 earthquake.
(Image credit: USGS)
Approximately 1,655 people died in the largest earthquake ever recorded, which struck Valdivia, Chile, on May 22, 1960. Thousands more were injured, and millions were left homeless. Southern Chile suffered $550 million in damage.
The quake triggered a tsunami that killed 61 people in Hawaii, 138 in Japan and 32 in the Philippines.
The earthquake struck where the Nazca Plate dives underneath the South American Plate, on the Peru-Chile Trench.
